question: Panama has held a yellow card, the EU’s formal warning that a country is not doing enough to stop illegal fishing, since December 2019. Panama says it has rewritten its fisheries law, hired inspectors, opened a monitoring centre and tightened controls at ports and processing plants. At this stage, one of Panama’s main priorities is the completion and implementation of its traceability system.

Its implementation is taking longer than expected owing to the technical, administrative and budgetary requirements associated with a system of this scope. Panama is no small partner: it runs the Panama Canal, flags more ships than other countries, and sits in a region the EU should have closer ties with. 1.
Will the Commission set out a clear timeline and the criteria that Panama still has to meet, and will it give the country the time it needs to finish its work on the traceability system?
What help can the Commission offer a country under a yellow card, and will it offer that help to Panama, so that this becomes a dialogue more about support and cooperation than about cards?
How does the Commission weigh this process against the EU’s strategic and trade interests in Panama and Latin America, while other global powers move into the region?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.10.2026) The Commission sends a roadmap to each third country together with the pre-identification decision. It reflects the shortcomings identified and the measures expected, providing the framework for assessing progress. This practice was also followed with Panama.

The dialogue between the Commission and pre-identified third countries is continuous and progress-based, without a predetermined deadline. Its duration depends on the nature of the shortcomings and the pace and effectiveness of the measures taken. The dialogue focuses on cooperation, technical engagement and sustainable improvements.

The Commission clarifies shortcomings and expected measures, provides guidance and expertise, and reviews progress. Countries are given reasonable time to implement reforms and demonstrate tangible progress. The responsibility for adopting, implementing and enforcing the necessary measures remains with third country authorities.

The Commission remains closely engaged with Panama and assesses progress based on evidence. The EU and Panama have a comprehensive and positive relationship under the EU-Central America Association Agreement1. Its trade pillar has been applied by both the EU and Panama since 2013, and the agreement including its political and cooperation pillar entered into force in 2024.

Sustainable development is an integral part of this relationship. Although the dialogue on illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing is conducted outside the Agreement’s institutional framework and under a separate legal basis, it supports shared objectives.
IUU fishing and other key aspects such as trade, investment and Global Gateway were discussed in the 2nd EU-Panama bilateral consultations held in October 20252.
